In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self-association of dsRBPs is conserved, but the mechanism of self-association differs between species and is influenced by the composition of the dimerization interface.
the dsRBD homomeric interactions are asymmetric in all cases examined.
the Type B dsRBP homodimerization mechanism is highly conserved, and that the structural asymmetry of these dimers may be important for their function in the miRNA pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dsRNA-binding domains of dsRBPs are not only capable of binding dsRNA but also capable of binding other dsRBD domains, and that this property is conserved from fruit flies to humans.
the dsRBD is a modular protein domain with two faces: one that interacts with dsRNA, and the other that interacts with proteins.
Type B dsRDBs homodimerize through an unusual mechanism in which a single dsRBD is involved and the homodimer is asymmetric.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dsRBD is an asymmetric homodimerization domain that has been co-opted for protein/protein interactions.
dsRBDs have been co-opted for a variety of protein/protein interactions in addition to RNA binding.
dsRBD homomeric assemblies are structurally asymmetric, and that this asymmetry is a conserved feature of dsRBDs that mediate protein/protein interactions.
